How to use AI for your medical studies.

One mistake many medical students make is trying to use one AI for everything.

I know this girl who'd upload a slide to ChatGPT and say, "Explain this to me like I'm a donkey." 😂

Funny prompt, but here's the problem.

There is no one-size-fits-all AI.

Each AI has strengths and weaknesses. Once you know what each one is good at, your studying becomes much easier.

Here are the ones I use.

1. NotebookLM — Best for understanding lecture slides and textbooks.

If your goal is to actually understand your lecturer's slides without AI bringing in too much outside information, NotebookLM is excellent.

Upload your slides and ask it to:

- Explain page by page.
- Summarize difficult concepts.
- Connect related topics.
- Generate an audio discussion you can listen to while walking.

It's one of the best learning tools available.

2. Perplexity — Best for research and analyzing questions.

If you're working through a past question and want evidence-based explanations or references, use Perplexity.

It's excellent for:

- Research.
- Finding reliable sources.
- Explaining why an answer is correct.
- Providing links to the original references.

Think of it as an AI search engine.

3. ChatGPT — Best for diagrams, anatomy charts, and medical graphics.

Need an anatomy chart?

A physiology flowchart?

A biochemistry pathway?

ChatGPT is currently one of the strongest image generators for educational graphics.

You can either upload your material or describe exactly what you want, and it will generate revision-quality charts.

4. Gemini — Best when you have lots of files.

Gemini is very generous with uploads.

If you have dozens of lecture slides or PDFs and want AI to work through them, Gemini handles large uploads very well.

It's also useful for generating summaries and flashcards from large sets of notes.

5. Evernote AI — Good for transcribing printed notes.

If you have handwritten or printed notes and want them converted into editable text, Evernote's AI features can help with transcription and organization.

6. Otter AI — Best for recording lectures.

Going for class?

Open Otter AI.

It records your lecturer, transcribes the lecture into text, and creates searchable notes you can review later.

Very useful if your lecturer talks fast.

7. Claude — Best for formatting notes and working through past questions.

Claude is excellent at:

- Organizing messy lecture notes.
- Turning slides into readable notes.
- Merging multiple lecture files into one document.
- Explaining past questions clearly and logically.

If you're preparing for MBBS professional exams, Claude saves a lot of time.

Finally, remember this:

Don't ask,

"Which AI is the best?"

Ask,

"Which AI is the best for this particular task?"

That's how you study smarter.

Use the right tool for the right job.

Reward-guided diffusion: reinforcement learning steers generative models toward novel, stable crystals

Anyone who trains generative models knows the tension. A diffusion model fit by maximum likelihood learns to reproduce its training distribution, so it samples what looks familiar. In materials discovery, though, the interesting compounds sit in the low-probability tails, the underexplored regions where genuinely new structures live. Sampling more of the same is exactly what you do not want.

Hyunsoo Park and Aron Walsh reframe this as a post-training problem. Instead of nudging outputs with heuristics like classifier-free guidance, they fine-tune the model with reinforcement learning, optimizing explicit rewards rather than data likelihood. The move that makes it tractable: they run diffusion in a compressed VAE latent space, which turns the awkward mix of discrete atom types and continuous coordinates into a homogeneous action space where policy gradients behave.

The engine is GRPO, the same group-relative policy optimization behind recent reasoning LLMs, here driving a denoising diffusion policy. The reward is multi-objective and, crucially, verifiable: a creativity term for uniqueness and novelty, a stability term using a machine-learning force field as a fast proxy for DFT energy above the convex hull, and a diversity term that blocks mode collapse.

The payoff is a clean shift of the Pareto frontier. On the Alex-MP-20 benchmark, their metastable-unique-novel score jumps from 15.9% to 61.3%, novelty climbs from 62.3% to 97.5%, and metastability still rises from 51.2% to 72.1%. Novelty and stability usually trade off, and here RL buys both at once. The same framework handles inverse design too: targeting a 3 eV bandgap, RL keeps chemical validity intact while classifier-free guidance collapses to near-zero.

For discovery pipelines in batteries, catalysis, or semiconductors, the practical takeaway is that a verifiable reward plus policy optimization can redirect a generative model toward candidates worth synthesizing, not merely plausible ones. Swap the reward and the same machinery targets ionic conductivity, formation energy, or a specific gap, giving a modular path from "generates something reasonable" to "generates what the program actually needs."

Paper: Park et al., Nature Machine Intelligence (2026), CC BY 4.0 | https://t.co/4cwgBOxl0F

A paper worth knowing about if you're into quant trading and generative AI:

TRADES: Generating Realistic Market Simulations with Diffusion Models

Authors: Berti, Prenkaj, Velardi (Sapienza University of Rome + TU Munich)

What's inside:
> A transformer-based diffusion model for generating orders in the Limit Order Book (LOB) - realistic simulation of the market order book
> Two key metrics - realism (how close it is to real market behavior) and responsiveness (how the market reacts to an agent's actions)
> Results: ×3.27 and ×3.48 improvement over SoTA on the predictive score across two stocks
> DeepMarket - the first open-source Python framework for deep-learning-based LOB simulations
> Comes with a synthetic LOB dataset generated by the model itself

A step toward backtesting trading strategies and training RL agents on data that behaves like a real market instead of random noise.

https://t.co/QGLOigO4cN

Fragments of Growth is a hand crafted art collection by @jenyavyguzov, a fashion photographer and visual artist whose work has appeared in Vogue, GQ Style, Elle, Tatler, L'Officiel, and campaigns for brands including Puma and IKEA.

Every artwork is built from real photographs taken over years of travel.

The team has also hinted at post-mint mechanics, including holder rewards and exclusive access to future 1/1 pieces from the artist's archive.

In a market filled with copy-paste projects, it's refreshing to see a collection built around genuine artistry and a story that feels personal.

Not very early, but definitely one I'm bullish on.

RL can't teach an LLM to solve problems it never solves. Robot policies suffer from exactly the same limitation.

The fix turned out to be almost embarrassingly simple: train the policy with diffusion noise during pre-training.

That's it.

The policy covers a much wider action distribution, RL finally has somewhere to search, and we fine-tune VLAs on real robots in under an hour.

Introducing TMRL.
